Homage to the Buddha.
Since the comprehension of objects that are beyond the reach of the senses depends upon inference, this work is commenced in brief for the purpose of explaining it.

The reason (hetu) is that which is a property of the subject (pakṣadharma) and is pervaded by a part of it; it is of only three kinds due to the restriction of invariable concomitance (avinābhāva). All others are fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa).
The "subject" (pakṣa) is the locus of the property (dharmin),
because the term for the whole is applied metaphorically to its part. If it is argued that this metaphorical usage is unjustified due to a lack of purpose, we say no.

Because the figurative designation (upacāra) has the purpose of negating the properties of all phenomena (dharmin), in this way visibility and so forth are excluded. Furthermore, by the word "property" (dharma), because a property depends on another, it necessarily implies its substratum, the possessor of the property (dharmin).

If it is argued that, because the property-bearer (*dharmin*) is mentioned in the proof, the property-bearer of the probandum (*sādhyadharmin*) is established due to proximity, we say no; for the example-bearer (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) is also proximate. Since its existence in the example-bearer is established through the pervasion by that part (*tadaṃśavyāpti*), [the mention of] the property-bearer [in the thesis] serves to establish the property-bearer of the probandum.

Inclusion (*parigraha*). Even though [the definition] is already established, the repetition might be suspected of being for the sake of restriction (*niyama*), such that existence (*sattva*) would apply only to the similar class (*sajātīya*). Even though that absence—namely, non-existence (*asattva*) in the case of the dissimilar class (*vyatireka*) where the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent—is already established, it is like the statement of non-existence; for by stating the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of that part [of the reason], [the definition] is established.

Furthermore, even if the property [of the probans] exists in the subject of the example, the explicit mention of the "subject" (dharmin) might be suspected of being intended to restrict its existence to that [subject] alone. Therefore, although the meaning is understood through implication, the mention of the "subject" is merely a figurative expression; by this uniform designation, the burden of comprehension is avoided.

If it is argued that because the property belongs to the subject (*pakṣadharma*), it depends on that qualification and thus does not extend elsewhere, resulting in the fallacy of being "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇatā*), we say no;
for the qualification functions by means of the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*).
Just as in the case of "Caitra is an archer," which excludes connection with others, it is not like "Pārtha is an archer," [which excludes non-connection].
That part is its property (*tad-aṃśas tad-dharmaḥ*).

Pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists either in the necessary presence of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) wherever the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is present, or in the presence of the pervaded only where the pervader is present.

By this, both positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), as well as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), are [established] according to their respective natures.
It is stated that [the reason] is ascertained by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
for in every case, if the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is absent in the reason,

the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established, or because there is an absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) when the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is excluded, [the reason must be established] through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*).
When both [the reason and its pervasion] are ascertained, the pervasion by that part [of the reason] is ascertained.
In that regard, the ascertainment of the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) within the locus of the probandum (sādhyadharmin) is its establishment through either direct perception or inference.

Just as, for example, smoke in a particular location, or the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) in sound. For one who has perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) a smoky location as having a form distinct from other objects— that is, as having its own unique nature— the object of that perception is the specific difference exactly as it was seen.
The cognition of a sign (liṅga) arises from memory.
Among these, that initial perception whose object is unique is alone the valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
When that [object] has been seen in such a state, whatever its unique [feature] may be, there arises—

by the force of perception and by grasping the form exactly as it was seen— a memory whose object is the exclusion of what is other (*atad-vyāvṛtti*), which expresses both the uniqueness of that [object] and its distinction from that [other]. It is not [produced] otherwise.

[It is] not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because for one who, having previously seen something uncommon, designates it as "uncommon," there is no apprehension of a new object; for although the accomplishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) was seen [previously],
the conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) does not subsequently apprehend that unperceived nature which is the means of accomplishing that action.

And it is like inference. For every discerning person seeking purposeful action investigates whether something is a means of valid cognition or not; and a universal does not perform any purposeful action whatsoever.

After the apprehension of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), one prepares [the object] as that which is to be grasped by the conceptualizing consciousness (*vikalpavijñāna*) produced through its power, such as when, having seen blue, there is the cognition "it is blue. For it is that very same specific characteristic of blue which performs such purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) as is to be accomplished.

And that [object] is indeed seen by him through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in its own nature. Furthermore, the purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by the object "blue"—which is the objective domain of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of "blue" arising at a time subsequent to the apprehension of that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—is not performed [by that conceptualization]. Therefore, [the conceptual construction] has as its object a thing not previously cognized.

Even the term "valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) must be qualified by the phrase "with respect to a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) not yet cognized. However, when the particular characteristic has already been cognized, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that arises through its power and conforms to it is merely a memory (*smṛti*), and not a valid cognition, because its object is [the particular] only indirectly through its effect.
Because an object that has not been apprehended is not apprehended,
since the establishment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is based upon an object.
Because those who seek it engage in activity toward an object that is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-yogya*),
for a real entity (*vastu*) is indeed characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency;
therefore, [one acts] toward the real entity even from that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
For activity proceeds precisely through the determination of that [object], since in its activity, conceptual construction shares the same success and security as perception.

If it is argued that because there is no difference in utility from the preceding moment of perception, it would follow that subsequent [moments] lack validity, we say no; for there is a desire for an object to be accomplished by a specific moment.

Because their acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) are diverse. For when an effect is common [to all], there is no difference in their capacity, just as in the case of fires proximate to smoke that is cognized through successive stages, regarding an object to be established merely by the presence of fire.
By this, the conceptualization of the property (*dharma*), the locus (*dharmin*), the mark (*liṅga*), and so forth, which follows upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [is explained].

The validity of future [states] has already been refuted. Furthermore, regarding the determination of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in the case of an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*), it consists in the fact that, by virtue of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) being in reality of the same nature as that [reason], it is necessarily connected to the mere existence of the proving property (*sādhanadharma*).
Establishment [of the reason] is the operation of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the reason when it is reversed from the probandum (*sādhya*).
For example: "Whatever exists is necessarily momentary, because if it were non-momentary, it would be contradictory for it to perform a causal function (*arthakriyā*)."
In that case, the nature of being a real entity (vastutva) would be lost. In the case of an effect-reason (*kāryahetu*), the causal relationship is established;
for example, when this [effect] is perceived, it is perceived despite having met the conditions for perceptibility and not having been perceived previously.
Even when other causes are present,

if this [cause] is absent, it does not occur; thus, the presence [of the effect] when that [cause] is present and its absence when that is absent— established through perception and non-perception— is the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).

Its establishment is as follows: for the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) itself would be established in this way for a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), such that wherever there is smoke, there is necessarily fire;
[this is] the presence of fire.
For the very existence of smoke is its being an effect of that [fire]. In the case of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) as well,

the determination of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is established by demonstrating the absence of any other cause for the application of the conventional designation "non-existent" (*asad-vyavahāra*), which occurs solely upon the non-apprehension of that which has met the conditions for apprehension.

The determination of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) for the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*) and the nature-reason (*svabhāvahetu*) is also established through the proof of the causal relation and the pervaded-pervader relation; specifically, it is taught that the non-existence of the reason when the probandum is absent is established by means of the non-perception of the cause and the non-perception of the pervader, both of which have perceptible objects as their domain.
In order to demonstrate the absence of the object;

otherwise, because the absence [of an object] would not be established in any instance for that which has met the conditions for non-perception (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*). [If it were] without a specified object, [it would apply] to the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*).

The demonstration of non-existence is established simply by proving the absence of a connection; therefore, in that case, when establishing the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), the requirement that the two types of non-perception have a perceptible object (*dṛśya-viṣayatā*) is not necessary. The ascertainment of negative concomitance in the case of non-perception [occurs] through the non-apprehension of something that, if it existed, would meet the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*).

The perception of non-existence. This reason, characterized by these [three], is indeed threefold; it is of only three types: essential nature (*svabhāva*), effect (*kārya*), and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). For example, when some impermanent thing is to be proven, existence (*sattva*) [is the reason].
In a place possessing fire there is smoke, and in its absence there is the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perception;

since the rule of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is restricted to these three cases alone, the aforementioned pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) is inseparable connection.
It is said to be restricted precisely to this [subject] because it does not exist elsewhere than in the three types of causes.
In that regard, [the reason] is that which follows the mere presence of the property to be proven (sādhya-dharma) through the presence of the proving property (sādhana-dharma).

The essential nature (*svabhāva*) is the logical reason (*hetu*). Even though there is a difference in properties (*dharma-bheda*) due to the distinction between successive exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*), in reality the reason is nothing other than the essential nature of the probandum (*liṅgi-svabhāva*), because there is no deviation from the positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*) within the nature of the reason.
Regarding the definition, the qualification by "concomitance with that alone" (*tan-mātra-anvaya*) takes into account the views of others.

For others indeed maintain that a property (*dharma*) which has another thing as its cause, even if it follows merely upon the absence of that [other thing], is an essential nature (*svabhāva*). By means of the qualification,
he states that such a thing is not an essential nature with respect to that probandum, and thereby points out the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of the reason (*hetu*) in that case, as follows:
When destruction has a cause, the property of being produced [serves as the reason].
Its application is twofold:
by way of similarity and by way of dissimilarity.
Just as "whatever is existent is all momentary, like a jar and so forth,
and sound is existent," so too, in the absence of momentariness there is an absence of existence, and sound is existent.

The two types of formal argument— those based on similarity and those based on dissimilarity— are characterized by the demonstration of pervasion (*vyāpti*) through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), encompassing all cases. In this regard,
since the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is understood through the force of these [concomitances] alone, there is no need for an explicit statement of the proposition.

The formal argument is as follows: If it is asked, "How can there be cognition of that object when the object of knowledge (*prameya*) has not been demonstrated?"—in the case of one's own realization, who is the demonstrator of the object of knowledge? For one who has perceived smoke located in a particular place, through the recollection of its pervasion by fire, [cognition arises] by the power of that [recollection].
In this case, the cognition "there is fire here" arises; yet no one informs him that "there is fire here," nor does he previously apprehend anything,
because in the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no cause for such a cognition.

If [the object] is already cognized, the logical mark (liṅga) is useless. Having established the object of cognition—namely, "there is fire here"—all by oneself and without cause, one subsequently follows the logical mark in order to cognize that [same thing]. What kind of sequence of cognition is this? Even according to the opponent...
That which is being stated indeed floats away,
because it lacks utility (*upayoga*). If it is argued that "utility" is the presentation of the object (*viṣaya*), [we reply:]...
What is the purpose of demonstrating that very [point] for now? If cognition were not otherwise, everything would be satisfactory. Therefore, this [point] itself—
Even without any [word] presenting an object,
having observed us acting, he clearly seeks a price, like a Brahmin at a festival;
for even from our speech, he follows the *liṅga* (probans) which is established in itself.

What is the difference between these two states, such that one "understands"? Furthermore, since it is observed that understanding occurs even without the statement of the thesis (pratijñā), based solely on the statement of the property of the subject (pakṣadharma) and the [logical] connection (sambandha), what is the utility of it? It is for the purpose of producing certainty in others just as one has attained certainty oneself.

And the means of proof (sādhana) is stated; therein, even without personally demonstrating the object of cognition (prameya), one who understands it himself and explains it to another [establishes] what was not previously known.
What is the reason for relying on the sequence of objects? Therefore, there is no purpose whatsoever in stating the objects of cognition (*prameya*), since comprehension occurs even otherwise.
Because [the probans] has already arisen.
By this, the application (*upanaya*), the conclusion (*nigamana*), and so forth, are also refuted;
for by this much alone [the proof is established].

Because the cognition of the probandum exists [even without it]. Setting aside your stubborn bias (*ḍiṇḍika-rāga*), close your eyes for a moment and consider: would there be such a cognition by this much alone, or not? If there were, what is the use of this garland of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*)?
Thus, in a syllogistic argument (*sādhana-vākya*), this much alone is the superior usage.
Furthermore, in this regard, there is no fixed rule regarding the sequence of the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and the statement of the [logical] connection (*sambandha*).
Someone [objects]: "In every way, because it is indicative;
even when the relation is stated, the usage of the term alone is distinct, in both cases."

Even though there is a difference in properties (*dharma-bheda*), it is nevertheless the manifestation of that very state [of being]. For the existence of something that does not have that intrinsic nature (*atat-svabhāva*) is not, as a rule, the existence of another thing, just as the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is not the state of being immediately following effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*).
Nor does the cessation of that which is not of the same nature entail the cessation of that which is not its effect,

as is the case with the cessation of these two very properties. Therefore, when either positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is employed according to its definition, it implies the other.
It implies that the employment of two [reasons] in a single probative statement is not desired,
because it would be redundant;
for when the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is established by the very nature of that [reason], the absence [of the probandum] is established by its absence.

Furthermore, since the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is established by the proof of non-existence when that [probans] is absent, the formulation of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)— even for the purpose of demonstrating the restriction that "non-apprehension occurs only in the absence of that [probans], and not elsewhere, nor in its contrary"— is not tenable.
Since even those things that are contradictory to one another are [considered] counter-examples (vipakṣa),
how is this understood— that existence necessarily has a perishable nature— by which the possibility of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) could arise? If this is asked:
Because a cause of destruction is impossible, entities are perishable by their very nature;
they do not [perish] through anything else once they have been produced.
The arising of destruction [is impossible] because that [destruction] lacks causal efficacy;
for the cause of destruction does not possess the intrinsic nature of an entity.

It does not perform [the function] in this way, because that [obscuration] has ceased. Nor is it simply another entity, for if it were to produce another entity while the original entity remains in its same state, it would perform nothing at all; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of its being perceived as such and so forth.
Nor is another entity its obscuration.

Because when it is in that state, even the obscuration is impossible. Nor is the non-existence of an entity produced by a cause of destruction; for if non-existence were accepted as a positive entity (vidhi), there would be the dilemma of its being either distinct or non-distinct [from the entity].

Because it does not transcend conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). If [destruction] were of a single nature consisting solely in the negation of existence, it would follow that "it does not produce existence";
and thus, being a non-agent, it would lack causality, and therefore it cannot be a cause of destruction.
Furthermore,
[the cause of destruction] would be useless. If an entity were by its own nature perishable and unstable in itself, it would have no need for causes of destruction.
Because it perishes by its very own nature; for whatever has such a nature arises from its own causes as being precisely of that kind.
Furthermore, it does not depend on another cause for its existence, just like substances such as light, fluidity, heat, and solidity; for light and the others,
having arisen as that very nature, do not require another cause for their state of being light and so forth.

If they were dependent [on something else], it would follow that they lack self-nature (*nairātmya*), because there would be an absence of identity (*tādātmya*) with that which constitutes their own nature.
Likewise, if a thing characterized by non-stability were established by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it would not require any further cause for that state of being its very essence.

If it is argued that there is no certainty [of a cause producing its effect] because of the case of seeds and the like, it might be as follows: although seeds and so forth possess the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of producing sprouts and the like, they depend upon other causes such as water; therefore, they do not [produce their effects] when alone.

Just as that [cause] produces [the effect], so too would an entity (bhāva) exist for the sake of destruction. This is not so, because that which has such a nature produces it, whereas that which does not produce it lacks that nature.
For this very reason, a difference between the entities in those two states must be determined.

Because there is no change in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of entities, that very same nature would entail their production even prior [to the final moment], just as it does later. Therefore, that which is the final particular state is itself the sprout and so forth.
The nature of production [belongs to the effect]. However, since the preceding specific states of the cause are themselves causes, there is no inconclusiveness [in the reason],
because in momentary entities, there is the arising of successive [states].
Because there is no unity [among them].
Why do those final [causes], being capable, not produce [the effect]? They certainly do produce it;
there is no other possibility here, because their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is not subject to change. This applies to all of them.

If it is asked, "When the auxiliary causes possess a capable nature, what further use is there for another [cause]?", we reply: entities certainly do not act with prior deliberation, such that others would desist on the grounds, "Since this one alone is capable, what need is there for us? Their operations are devoid of intention.

For those things whose nature consists in being deposited through the transformation of their own causes, being such by virtue of that very nature, do not deserve censure. If it is asked, "Why do they not produce [their effects] one after another?", the answer is no, because their capacity exists only for the production of that single [effect]. It is for the production of that one alone.
If it is argued that because [the cause] is capable of producing nothing else, there is no successive production,
and that when a single effect arises from auxiliary causes such as the eye which possess distinct intrinsic natures, there would be no difference in the effect despite the difference in the causes;

No, because through the distinction of their respective intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), there is a non-confusion of the specific nature of the effect resulting from that application, due to the application of those specific qualities—
just as in the case of a lump of clay and a potter.
The nature of a jar arising from clay-lumps—
which are distinct from threads and other such things— is different from those [threads] because they lack the nature of clay;
and while that very thing exists as clay, its nature as a specific configuration is distinct from others because of the thread.
The wheel and so forth possess a distinct nature from that very [clay] which consists of a particular configuration;
thus, in this way, the nature of clay does not come from the potter, nor does the particular configuration belong to the clay.
Nor is there a difference in the nature of the effect produced by those two, even though there is a difference in their specific capacities and objects;
for the clay and the shape, being non-identical with one another, [would otherwise] possess the nature of both shape and clay.
Because it would follow that those two would not appear [together].
Shape is indeed something other than the substance of clay as a quality;
therefore, it is distinct from it.
If it is argued that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the object of utility for both the potter and the lump of clay, this has already been addressed.
Furthermore, if the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) were distinct from the clay, what would the potter do?

It does not separate them. Because a quality is dependent upon a substance, it does not separate them. If that substance, by its very nature, consists of the locus of that configuration, or if that configuration consists of being supported by it, [then they are not distinct].
If it is asked, "Is it in dependence upon the potter?
No, because from that [potter] there is the acquisition of the capacity for mutual relation;
otherwise, since capacity is the very nature (*dharmatā*) of the entity itself, the shape of the lump of clay would have existed even prior [to the potter's action].

If there is the capacity for a specific relation, then there follows the contingency of a relation with a specific configuration. In that case, since that capacity of the clay-substance arises from the potter, there is no difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of these two.
For if there were a difference [between the two], the same consequences as before would follow.

There certainly exists, even in the case of something possessing a single nature, the quality of having specificities imparted by multiple conditions; therefore, this does not serve to prove that clay and its shape possess a single nature.
01018 Persistence.

01019 Therefore, the auxiliary conditions do not have a single application-object (*upayoga-viṣaya*), even though the nature of the effect is one in reality; thus, as here, there is a difference in causes for [effects that are] distinct—

Because it serves a specific purpose, it should not be inferred that [the sense organ] has the same function as the eye and so forth in the production of consciousness. For instance, from the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya), which is consciousness, the nature of apprehension (*upalambhātmatā*) of visual consciousness arises; and that very nature of apprehension [belongs to that consciousness].

The specific capacity of the existent visual faculty to grasp form is determined by the object; that [capacity] consists in its having a form similar to that [object]. Thus, although the effect is in fact non-different from its causes, distinct particularities arise precisely from the distinct intrinsic natures (svabhāva) of those causes. Therefore, it is not the case that...

Even when there is a difference in causes, there is no difference in that specific effect. These very same differences in the causal potencies are present, with their powers unimpeded, for the production of their respective distinct effects; because of momentariness, this is the nature of the effect of the causal complex.
They are called the basis for persistence. For in this way, from all those [elements] together,
there arises a single entity with a distinct nature, consisting of perception, the grasping of form, and the specific determination of the objective form.

If it is asked: "In the case of momentary conditions which possess unobstructed power, whose effects follow immediately, and to which no further excellence can be added, what is the meaning of their 'cooperation' (sahakāra) with one another?"—it is not the case that cooperation everywhere consists in the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*). What then? It is that which [occurs] among many...
Even the performance of a single purpose,
as in the case of the final collection of causes,
is the primary state of being a cooperative cause for those cooperating factors.
Because that very last [moment] is the cause, and because in that state it is impossible to produce a distinction due to the non-differentiation of the single nature of the moment.
Because the production of a particularity is characterized by the arising of a different intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

If there were the production of a different entity (*bhāva*), there would be no final [moment], and consequently, it would not be the direct cause. Therefore, there is no particularity produced in the cause by its auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*).

This is their arising. Those final conditions, which are capable by their very nature, arise simultaneously; they are momentary, such that there is no prior, posterior, or separate existence among them, and immediately following which the effect is produced.
In this regard, cooperation (*sahakāritva*) consists precisely in the performance of a single purposeful action (*eka-arthakriyā*).
If it is asked, "From what is that which is capable produced?"
From their own causes.
Why do those [causes] produce this [effect] when other conditions are not present?
For they might sometimes act otherwise.

And if it is argued that even a single [cause] might produce [an effect] in some instance, [we reply]: although the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*), possessing distinct capacities at every moment through their connection with successive conditions,
continue as a continuum and appear similar due to some degree of uniformity;
Even though they are perceived [in this way], their intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is nonetheless distinct;
therefore, something...
Thus, for something [to arise], there must be a cause.

In that regard, the collection of factors such as form and the sense-faculty, which exists in a location characterized by lack of obstruction and so forth, is the cause capable of producing consciousness. As for their mutual approach—
The first substratum is a specific condition (*pratyaya-viśeṣa*); it is capable of producing those causes.

Since their existence does not occur prior to, after, or separately [from one another], the defects that arise from priority, posteriority, and separateness do not attach to them, even though they are capable. Therefore, that which...

The cause for their mutual approach and so forth is that [cause] which is capable; thus, in that case, there is never any deviation from its nature. By this principle, the specific determination of the relationship between cause and effect everywhere should be understood as consisting of distinct natures at every moment.
[This applies] to the capacities of entities which follow upon differentiation,
but not to entities that possess a stable and unitary nature,
because it is impossible for a nature to undergo change; [for] those things whose natures are either capable or incapable [of action].
Because neither action nor non-action is possible.
If it is argued that [the agent] acts when accompanied by another and not alone,
then what is the function of the one acting alone?

If it is argued that its nature is either capable or incapable of producing [an effect], and that it is indeed capable, then why does it not produce it? If it does not produce it, how can it be said to be capable? If it is argued that weavers and others, though capable of the action of producing cloth and so forth, do not perform it at all times—
A fool who delights in play, dear to the gods, brought up in luxury, even though [instructed] again and again.
This has already been thoroughly examined in the discussion introducing the seed and so forth. Therefore,
since a change in intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is impossible, the persistence of that which possesses such a nature must be unavoidable, just as it is in its final state.
In the final state, when capacity arises for that which was previously incapable,
if that capacity is of the same nature [as the entity], it is simply the production of something new; if it is not of that same nature...
It is indeed a non-agent,
because the production of the effect arises from that which is called "capacity" (sāmarthya).
Furthermore, why does that very [entity], when accompanied by all its auxiliary causes (sahakārin), produce the effect?
One is seen acting while performing;
therefore, we say that he acts. Oh, what great capacity!
What great power is this, that one perceives even those entities that do not possess that very nature!

The employment [of things] in various functions by means of their mere intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-mātra*). Even if, by some chance, something were to occasionally transcend the path of perception here, alas, it would be of a nature that does not produce [anything further] and its continuity would have ceased; such is this [view].

"Anxiety distresses the mind. Indeed, we do not claim that things which lack that intrinsic nature (svabhāva) perform their causal function merely by virtue of our perception of them. Rather, it is by their very intrinsic nature that they possess the property of performing those functions.
Perceiving them, we know only that "these are the causal factors. True,
this too is the case.

Their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) consists in the property of performing an action as an effect; therefore, for those possessing all the necessary conditions, it is not a fault to fail to produce [the effect] through neglect.
Is that intrinsic nature, which possesses the property of non-delayed action, [present] in them at that very moment, or is it final?
Does it arise in that state, or did it exist even previously? It existed;
for those things whose nature is stable, single, and characterized by neither falling away nor arising, there can never be an absence of any of their inherent natures.

Because of the contradiction. Is it then that a woman is both a mother and barren? Or what is the meaning of this statement: "The nature [of the entity] possesses the property of performing the action of throwing, yet it does not perform it"?
If you say that its nature is [to act] only when conjoined [with other factors] and not when alone, [we reply:]...
In that case, the solitary [entity] is one thing and the combined [entity] is another;
for a difference in intrinsic nature is the defining characteristic of a difference in entities.
For even when in conjunction with others, he does not act by means of another's form;
and since his own nature remains exactly the same as it was before, how could there ever be a cessation of activity? This is also the case for one who holds that [the self] exists.
Why does that [momentary entity] not act alone?
If it were [present], it would certainly act.
Why is it not present? Because of its momentariness. It has been stated what kind of [entity] performs the action; how then [could it act otherwise]?

That which is produced in a single moment would become otherwise. And that which comes into being is precisely that which does not come into being; thus, this undesirable consequence does not apply, because the intrinsic natures of the agent and the non-agent are distinct.
Because of the contradiction with the reason.
Even for one who thinks that its very nature consists solely in the property of performing an action without delay,
that [nature] does not depend upon association.
But since an effect depends upon other conditions,
it arises from [causes] only when they are combined, not from them alone;
how then can that [cause] produce the effect even when it is alone, and yet the effect does not arise from it?

Thus, the contradiction remains as it was. If you say that it does not merely "act" [but acts in a specific way], then how can it now have the nature of non-delayed action? Is this not precisely what is being elucidated by the statement "it indeed acts"?
Moreover, how could this [agent], being capable even alone, disregard another who is looking for assistance? Disregarding the other, he would simply perform this task by force.
For in this way, he demonstrates his own capability:
by stating that "the effect depends on something else," it is expressed that [the effect] does not arise from that [cause] alone.

You claim that even in its solitary state, it possesses a nature capable [of producing the effect], and thus its production [of that effect] occurs from it; yet how could these two states coexist in one and the same thing? Therefore, this person—his vital points being pierced by the thorn of envy—is crying out in distress, and he deserves to be ignored.
Therefore, this co-operation, characterized by the performance of a single purposeful action, belongs only to momentary entities,
and not to non-momentary ones, for which separate existence is possible.
Because it is impossible to establish a rule of auxiliary causality (sahakāritva) based on the occurrence of separate actions.
However, in cases where entities attain the status of causes through the assistance of a continuum (santāna)—
as, for example, when rice seeds and the like produce boiled rice and sprouts with the aid of fire and water— [auxiliary causality is possible].
Regarding earth and the other elements,
the "cooperative activity" of conditions is said to be the production of a specific quality therein by means of a continuum as its basis.
Not by means of a substratum of substance,
because no distinction arises in a substance that is momentary.

For indeed, if no excellence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvātiśaya*) were produced sequentially in rice and other grains through burning and so forth, there would be no production of cooked rice and the like; nor, for one whose sense-faculties have entered a dark room from a luminous space, would there be the [perception of] an object if no specific transformation in the continuum (*santānaviśeṣa*) were produced by those factors that assist it.
[This is] the arising of practice.
However, in the case of the sense faculties and so forth, which act without delay, there is no production of excellence through mutual interaction.
In that regard, those [factors] which, by means of their respective conditions based on mutual approach and so forth, [arise...]

When they have reached a state where the place and other conditions are suitable, they attain the status of being causes for cognition along with the perfection of their own nature; thus, in that case, cooperation consists precisely in the performance of a single purposeful action.

In a case where cooperative conditions (sahakāri-pratyaya) produce a specific transformation, the causal continuum depends upon those conditions; therefore, it is said that it acquires a different intrinsic nature (svabhāvāntara). In that process, through the natural course of things, when the preceding moment of the causes and conditions ceases—
From those very [causes], through the production of successive distinguished moments, there eventually arises from the final complex of causes— possessing excellence— the production of the effect.
Regarding the production of the effect from a cause that has acquired excellence through its auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*), [the opponent argues] that this excellence...

In this way, origination is not logical. If a specific quality were to arise from that which is undifferentiated, it would follow that the effect [could likewise arise] from that which is undifferentiated;

furthermore, even auxiliary causes that depend on the production of mutual specific qualities would produce the effect. Consequently, even non-momentary things would possess causality independently of auxiliaries.

[If that were so,] there would be no production of an excellence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-atiśaya*) from the factors to be depended upon. Alternatively, if [it is argued that] the entity itself, having been made distinct by the auxiliaries, would remain present for the production of that distinction;
in that case, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, the auxiliaries are not [inherently] conducive to the production of each other's effects.
Because they would always remain in a state capable of producing a particular quality (*viśeṣa*), such that a mutual particularity produced by them would be eternally attached [to them],
there would be no manifestation of the effect upon the presence or absence of those means.
Because separation is observed. If it is argued that, for this reason, the first particularity does not arise from the auxiliary causes for that which receives no assistance, we reply:
no, for there is nothing gained by our repeating ourselves again and again.
There arises a sense of alarm;
if, even so, there is a logical understanding among people, then indeed let it be said: it is not solely from the production of a specific quality that auxiliary causes [act].
Because they possess the state of being co-operative causes, in the absence of which [state] there would be no co-operative causes for the production of a particular effect.
What then? [They are co-operative causes] even for a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyā*). That too would occur among things that are devoid of mutual distinction. Now, if it were so...
If it is argued that [the effect] might also exist separately, and thus that effect which arises from a specific [cause] could also arise from [that cause] alone;
At every moment,

through various successive conditions, there arises a specific transformation within the continuum of an entity; this includes the production of effects by those specific states such as being in a suitable location, and from which [these effects arise].
Even though each [cause] possesses individual capacity, there is no action [of the effect] from them alone, just as [there is no action] from [seeds] individually;
furthermore, because there is no separate existence of a specific agent, the effect is twofold:
one characterized by the production of a succession of specific qualities generated by auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), and another, such as the sprout and so forth.

Thus, everything has been stated: because of the difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of cause and effect, just like [the case of] a sense-faculty (*indriya*) that does not project [its own cognition] and its corresponding sensory consciousness (*vijñāna*). In that regard, when the production of an effect from causes depends upon the assistance of a continuum (*santāna*) provided by auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), the first distinction among those auxiliaries is the [auxiliary factor itself].
That which has been produced by a specific [cause] does not arise immediately, like an effect that follows without interval;
rather, those specific qualities that arise from that point onward are born from that [specific cause].
Because that [effect] and those [causes] possess that nature,

there is no infinite regress. Likewise, if even a non-momentary entity were to produce an effect without generating an excellence (atiśaya), just like the initial specific cause, [then it would follow that it could produce all effects at once].
Let it indeed do so;
for that is its very nature,
provided that its property is not to produce [the effect] without delay.

It has been stated that because separate existence is possible, even a solitary [entity] might be so; however, even then, that which does not possess that nature is simply non-productive. Therefore, for non-momentary causes, there is no [capacity] whatsoever through a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyā*).
Nor is there a restriction on its being a cooperative cause by virtue of assisting a continuum; thus, it has no cooperative cause whatsoever.

Therefore, even in isolation, it would produce [its effect]. However, for the most part, a continuum of entities existing in an aggregate state, having acquired specific qualities produced by cooperative conditions, performs its own effect.

It is observed, as in the case of seeds and the like. For one who maintains that the cause is stable, it is evident that when there is dependence on conditions (*pratyaya*), there is the production of another intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) for the causal agent; this is what is meant by "dependence on the effect."
It is said: It is not logical for an agent that possesses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) to exist prior to its activity.
Therefore, whatever has a certain nature is of that very character by virtue of its mere existence (*sattāmātra*);
it does not, having come into being, depend upon further external conditioning (*parābhisaṃskāra*) to become that which it is, because of its own intrinsic nature.
For an entity whose nature is non-abiding, there is nothing whatsoever to be effected by causes of destruction;
likewise, for an entity whose nature is abiding, what use are causes of destruction?
Because it is impossible for anyone to alter an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), or else, if such alteration were admitted, that very thing would not possess that intrinsic nature; thus,
it remains the same alternative as before.

And it has been stated therein: "That which is a change from another is a different intrinsic nature (svabhāva); and how can that which is different belong to it? For the distinction between entities is characterized by a distinction in their intrinsic natures. And thus, the former...

An entity that abides in the nature of non-decay does not undergo alteration. By this, the arising of a different intrinsic nature—such as liquidity—in hard substances like copper and the like due to fire and so forth is refuted; for even in those cases, the preceding state ceases through its own inherent nature (*svarasa-nirodha*).
Upon the destruction [of the previous state] by fire and so forth, and due to the material cause (*upādāna*), an entirely different nature characterized by fluidity and so on is produced;
that [new nature] is itself inherently subject to the property of duration.
Because it persists when a cause for destruction is absent,
its destruction must come from something else; yet destruction is not some other distinct intrinsic nature (svabhāva).

If it is argued that destruction is simply the cessation of existence (*bhāva-cyuti*), this answer does not transcend the following two alternatives: Is existence eternal by its own nature, or is it impermanent?

One who asserts that a thing, having been eternal in the past, subsequently becomes non-eternal, declares that there is a distinction between the eternally intended nature and the non-eternal nature at all times,
as well as two distinct entities, and furthermore, that it both perishes and does not perish.

In the former case, the cause of destruction is incapable [of acting]. It does not first exist as permanent and later become impermanent. What then? It remains permanent even later, because it possesses a single, uniform nature.
In that case, how can an entity be said to have perished if it does not enter into destruction by its very nature?
For that [entity] and its nature, as well as destruction, are not of a mutually identical form.
Therefore, if there is such destruction of it, it must exist by way of this nature of destruction.
Even so, it has been stated that a cause of destruction is useless. Therefore, whether an entity is by its very nature perishable or imperishable, there is no utility for a cause of destruction.
Consequently, an entity is independent with respect to its destruction; thus, whatever exists is necessarily determined to have that [destruction] as its nature.
That which exists is perishable; and with the cessation of perishability, there is the cessation of existence— thus is the establishment of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).

If it is argued that even though things are perishable by their very nature (*svabhāva*), something might still exist that does not have that nature—since not everything is the nature of everything—and therefore the establishment of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is not achieved; [we reply: no, because if things were non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*), they would necessarily follow as being non-entities (*avastu*). For efficacy (*śakti*) is the defining characteristic of an entity (*bhāva-lakṣaṇa*).

The absence of all causal capacity is the defining characteristic of non-existence. Furthermore, no capacity whatsoever can exist in a non-momentary entity, because such an entity lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) both successively and simultaneously. Therefore, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established: whatever is existent is necessarily momentary.
When another object is to be understood, the effect is the reason for the effect,
because it is non-deviant.
If the indicative power of the mark consists in its being related as cause and effect, then [it must hold] in every respect.

If it is argued that the relationship between the signifier and the signified (*gamyagamakabhāva*) exists in every respect because of the relationship between the produced and the producer (*janyajanakabhāva*), we say no;

for in the absence of that [causal relationship], there would be no necessity regarding the arising of the one from the other. Therefore, whatever effects are invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvin*) with as many essential properties (*svabhāva*) as exist in the cause, [those properties...]
It is the cause, because of the necessity of being its effect;
and it is by those very properties that [the effect] does not exist without them. If it is argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence of partial causality and causedness, we say no.
Because it is accepted that there is the apprehension of specific qualities produced by that [cause], and because the universals (sāmānya) are themselves adjuncts (upādhi) of specific marks (liṅga),
[the definition] is not intended when one wishes to speak of universals in their non-specific form, due to the fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra).
Even though something may arise from something else at some time for someone, everything of that kind is of such a nature.

If it is asked, "How is it determined that [the effect] arises from birth [of the cause]? and if it is further argued that "therefore, there is neither positive concomitance (anvaya) nor negative concomitance (vyatireka)," we say:

no. For that which does not arise from that [cause] would never arise from it even once. Cause and effect are characterized by the nature of producer and produced in mutual dependence. In that regard, if...
Smoke might arise from something other than the causal complex consisting of fire and so forth;
if it did not possess a nature produced by that [complex], it would not arise from it even once, just like any other distinct entity.

Nor can that causal complex (sāmagrī) produce it, because its nature is not to produce that [effect], just like any other causal complex. Furthermore, it is not logical for smoke to possess a nature that is both produced by that [complex] and not produced by it.
Because it possesses a single nature. If that which has the nature of producing both smoke and non-smoke were to arise, it would possess the nature of both smoke and non-smoke,
since the natures of effects are produced by the natures of their causes.

Furthermore, if one were not dependent on a cause, it would follow that there is no causality at all. Therefore, that which produces smoke is a specific causal complex consisting of fire and other factors; that which [consists of] the causal complex of fire and other factors—

That smoke is produced from a specific [cause]; for there is such a restriction of the nature of cause and effect that it does not arise from something of a different kind. Thus, that effect does not deviate from its cause. Therefore, when the relationship of cause and effect is established, [the inference] of the effect—
By this reason, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established.

Now, is it not observed that something arises even from a heterogeneous cause (*vijātīya*), such as the *śālūka* lotus from cow dung and the like? It does not arise from a heterogeneous cause; such [an instance] is—

For such [a color] has that very [cow-dung] as its primary cause; thus, there is no difference in the cause. However, in its continuous occurrence, it arises from the arrow. And even though there is no difference in the form (rūpa), there exists a difference in the nature of being produced from cow-dung versus something else.
For the mere similarity of form is not the sole cause for the reality of entities,
since even some things that possess non-different forms are distinguished from others by virtue of a specific difference.

Because we observe a difference in genus (*jāti-bheda*). For otherwise, if a non-distinct effect were produced even from a distinct causal complex (*sāmagrī*), then the distinction and non-distinction of effects would not follow from the distinction and non-distinction of their causes; consequently, the distinction and non-distinction of the entire universe would be without cause. Likewise...
For indeed, difference does not arise from difference, nor does non-difference arise from non-difference;
and since there is no nature of an entity whatsoever apart from those two, entities would be eternal due to their lack of a cause.
It would be either existent or non-existent,
because of the absence of anything to be depended upon. For it is through dependence that entities become occasional and possess a fixed determination regarding their effects.

There would be no restriction regarding the means of accomplishment (*sādhana-niyoga*). For, if the causal capacity were restricted, only a specific thing would be employed for the accomplishment of a particular result,
and nothing else.

Because that [cause] alone possesses the capacity for that [effect] while another lacks it, there is a distinction between the two due to their having natures that respectively produce that effect or its opposite.

Even if that [effect] were to arise from something whose nature is distinct from the nature of producing it, there would be no restriction regarding the power to produce it; consequently, it could arise from just anything whatsoever. However, if there is an identity in the power to produce it, then it is indeed that [specific cause]; thus, the observed effect does not deviate from its cause.
The non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension is either the cause of non-existence or the cause for the conventional usage of non-existence.
In this context, since apprehension is a property of the apprehending subject, apprehension is the cognition of that [object].

Therefore, the non-apprehension [of an object] is the apprehension of something else; because it is other than the apprehension intended [as the object], it functions as a relative negation (*paryudāsa*), like [the terms] "non-eatable" or "untouchable. [This applies to] that which is being apprehended—
In the case of being a dharma, apprehension is the nature of the object characterized by its fitness for producing a cognition of itself;
this is because fitness is of the nature of a positive entity (bhāva). Therefore, it is other than apprehension—
Non-perception is simply fitness (yogyatā), as in the previous case. When one thing is being perceived,
that which necessarily becomes perceived because there is no distinction in their fitness is conjoined with it.

Because of their association within a single cognition. When those two exist, there can be no cognition restricted to a single form, because that is impossible. Therefore, [the cognition arises] from those two whose forms possess undifferentiated capacity.
In this context, "otherness" (anyatva) is intended as a mutual dependence between two things associated within a single cognition,
because of the reliance on their proximity. That [object] alone,
in relation to that [cognition], is "other than it"— whether it be the cognition of it, its own nature, or the property of the knower and the known.

This is the non-perception of the characteristic (*lakṣaṇānupalabdhi*). It establishes either the absence of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) or the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of its absence.
How is it that the existence of another thing constitutes the absence of that [specific] thing?
If it is argued that by means of this non-perception of the form of non-existence one would establish the conventional usage of non-existence,
it has already been stated in this regard how [this is not so] in the case of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*).

Non-existence and non-apprehension are [defined] by way of their occurrence through dependence; it is not mere negation, because that would entail the failure to establish the means of proof and the failure to establish the conventional usage of non-existence. For that [non-existence], which has a nature unassociated [with existence], the establishment of another entity is itself the establishment of its non-existence.

The establishment [of one thing] is designated as the "absence of that" even when it is the existence of another. An entity characterized by the existence of another, being itself established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), would establish the conventional usage of the absence of that [other]; or, the absence of that is established by the establishment of that [existence].
There is no distinction whatsoever by which there would be a contradiction in establishing the conventional usage of non-existence through non-perception.
That very presence of another thing and the perception having that as its object constitute the non-existence of that [other] thing.
Why is it not a proof?
If you ask, "Is it not simply that the establishment of the existence of another thing is itself the establishment of its absence? [we reply: No.
And there is no relation because of the absence of non-separable establishment (*apṛthaksiddhi*).
First of all, the existence of another thing (*anyabhāva*) is not a means of proof; for when one thing is established, if the other is not established, [it cannot be said to be related].

That becomes its indicative mark (*liṅga*), like smoke [is for] fire. Through the very establishment of the existence of another, the non-existence of that [object] is established; for by the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that determines the reality of that [object] as having a nature unassociated with anything other than itself, the [non-existence of the other] is established.
Because exclusion is established,
and because of the absence of a relationship. And if that were its logical mark (liṅga), there would have to be some kind of relationship between it and that [mark].

Just as there is a co-inherence in a single substrate between producedness and impermanence, or between smoke and the possessor of the mark (the fire), whether it be a relation of container and contained,
or a relation of producer and produced— such [a relation] does not exist at all between existence and non-existence.
There is no relation by which this [cognition] could have a means of proof (*sādhana*).
If it is argued that there exists a subject-object relationship (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*), just like the relation between a word and its object, [we reply: regarding the word—

If there were an intention to convey those two objects, their employment [of words] would entail a relationship with them characterized either as cause and effect or as inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
However, since this is not possible in this case, how could there be a relationship of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*)?
For only when the relationship between the two as that of the probandum and the probans is established can the relationship of object and subject occur by means of it;
that very [relationship] is not established in the absence of a connection,
and if that is unestablished—
Nor is there a relationship of object and subject [between the absence and its locus], for otherwise this would result in mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

Furthermore, if non-existence were established through the existence of something else, then the non-aggregate [of the locus] would be what is proven. In that case, since the absence of a jar is [established] from the existence of something other than it, [the absence of the jar] would exist everywhere.

And [if that were so], there would be non-existence at all times. If it is argued that this is not the case because non-existence is established by means of a locus (dharmin) such as a specific location; [we reply: it is non-existence as a qualification of the locus—such as a specific location—that is being established, and not...

It is [the absence] alone; therefore, it is not the case that a non-collective entity is the probandum (*sādhya*). Nor is there a lack of connection between the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*), because the absence of another is connected with the locus (*dharmin*) such as a particular place and so forth—so he thinks. No, [that is not correct].
Because the absence of another consists precisely in the location and so forth.
For that very location where it is said "that which does not exist" is itself the absence of another, being unconnected with it.
Since the conceptual construction "this jar does not exist" arises from the perception of that [location] alone, how could it be [the absence] of that very [jar]?
This is the relationship between the mark (liṅga) and that which possesses the mark (liṅgin).
Furthermore, in this case, it is not possible to conceive of a relationship of generality and particularity,
such that the general property would be the reason (hetu) and the particular subject (dharmin) would be the locus.

Because the absence of that [object] is cognized precisely through the cognition of its specific counterpart, and because that [counterpart] does not exist elsewhere [where the absence is asserted], and because it constitutes a part of the very meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*),
it cannot function as a logical reason (*hetu*). Furthermore, it is not the case that wherever there is merely a location...

In that case, there is the absence of the jar. If it is argued that "absence" refers simply to such a bare location, [we reply: surely that very "bareness" is the "absence of the jar. And that is established precisely upon the cognition of the location which serves as the logical mark (*liṅga*). Of what, then, is that the mark? It is the mark of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
And following [the object] would be purposeless. Therefore, the existence of another thing is not a means of proving non-existence.
There is, however, a relationship consisting of contradiction.

If it is argued that the establishment of non-existence follows from the existence of another, then by what is there a contradiction of what? [It would be] of the counter-correlate (pratiyogin) by means of the existence of another.

What indeed is intended to be cognized as the counter-positive (pratiyogin), such that there would be a contradiction between the mark (liṅga) and the marked (liṅgin) and thus a [necessary] connection? Non-existence (abhāva), however, is not contradicted by the existence of another thing (anyabhāva) with respect to its counter-positive, the jar.

Because they coexist. How could there be a contradiction between the mark (liṅga) and the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) regarding that object of cognition? Therefore, there is an absence of a relationship. In this case as well, the fact that the collection [of properties] is what is to be proven remains unchanged.

If it is objected: "But surely, if there is no relationship between the existence of another thing and the non-existence of that [other], then the cognition of the non-existence of that thing could not occur through the cognition of the existence of another," we reply: No, for it does not arise from any such relationship.
The existence of another thing is accepted as that which makes known the absence of a given thing;
however, the existence of the other thing is itself the absence of that thing.

As stated previously: because the determination of that very essence—which is of an exclusive nature, unmixed with anything else, solitary, and established as a single self—is itself the exclusion of others, its solitude is the deficiency of another; thus, it is the existence of what is other than that.
The absence of that [object] is precisely the cognition of something other than it; and the non-cognition of that [object] is precisely the cognition of something other than it.
Otherwise, if there were no exclusion of another from that which has been delimited, [the two would be indistinguishable].
There would be no discernment of that [object] at all,

because there would be no distinction between what has that nature and what does not. This worldly transaction— which, upon seeing something, aims for the attainment or avoidance of it— [would not occur].
It would not be so. For even while perceiving fire, one does not perceive fire alone,
such that a person seeking water would not act [toward it].
If it is argued that the absence of water is cognized through non-perception (*anupalambha*),
then what is this so-called "non-perception"? If it is the absence of the perception of water, [then...]
How can that non-existence be the apprehension of something, or the cause of apprehension?
And how could that [apprehension] also [be so]?
If there is no cognition of that [object], or of anything else whatsoever,
or if there is a cognition of its non-existence, why is its non-existence not also perceived during states such as sleep, intoxication, fainting, interruption, or being turned away? Furthermore...
This has been examined in the *Pramāṇaviniścaya*. Therefore, one who perceives fire but does not ascertain, "This is fire, not water," would neither remain nor proceed;
thus, he would have fallen into an insurmountable calamity.
If it is argued that the cognition of the absence of another arises precisely from the perception of one,
how does the perception of one cause the understanding that "the other does not exist"? If it is replied that this is due to the perception of the [object] alone (*kevala*), [we respond as follows:]
This very point has been stated by us;
why does it appear harsh to you? Therefore, wander like a bird that does not see the shore.
Furthermore, one need not concern oneself with the direction toward which one must return— that is, with a direction that lacks any established basis.
If the exclusion of one thing is established simply through the determination of another, then this applies to everything.

The proof of non-existence would apply to another thing without distinction, and not only to that which is in an equivalent state of being perceptible; for it is the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*) that establishes non-existence.
Thus, the qualification need not be stated,
because even those things that have reached the conditions for non-perception are excluded there; for by the determination of one nature, the nature of anything other than that is [excluded].

Exclusion [is established] from a cognition whose appearance is restricted to that very nature; for the nature of one thing cannot be the nature of another. If there were no exclusion of other natures, there would be no purposeful activity [toward a specific object].

The previous undesirable consequence was that there would be an absence of the two exclusions (*nivṛtti*). However, the cognition, perceiving that [object] through its own nature as restricted by place, time, intrinsic nature, and state, excludes its deviation from that very state. For in this way, it is delimited by that [cognition].
If the state of being otherwise is excluded, and that very thing— and not something else— possesses the state of being as it is, then by excluding what has become otherwise,
it determines that [object]. Such is the operation of a single means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) with respect to all [objects].
He establishes entities in two groups,
because [the definition] is effective solely as the cause for the cognition of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

The absence of any other alternative is established precisely because pervasion is proven through the exclusion of everything else distinct from that [subject]; for if it were other than that, there would be an absence of pervasion.
Because that [means of valid cognition] does not exclude that object, there would follow the consequence that the existence [of the object] is not determined.
Therefore, when a means of valid cognition operates upon something,
it determines that, excludes what is other than that, and [establishes] the absence of a third alternative.

It indicates [the object]; thus, this is the operation of a single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, when a means of valid cognition operates in a certain case, it excludes that very object from others, precisely because of its own determination (*pariccheda*) thereof.
And it excludes precisely that which is other than that,

because there is no exclusion of anything else therein. Therefore, that very means of valid cognition establishes the absence of any other mode [of existence], since everything not seen when that is being seen is [necessarily] other than it.
Because of the establishment [of one thing] and the establishment of that which is other than it as being precisely that [thing].
By this, succession, non-succession, and so forth—which consist of mutual exclusion—are also explained.
Thus, from the perception of one thing, there is the exclusion of its opposite nature.
There is no exclusion of all other entities from that place and time;
therefore, it would both not have that nature and yet occupy that place and time,
like taste, color, and so forth.
Therefore, it is from non-apprehension exactly as described that the non-existence of something, somewhere, and at some time, is established.
Furthermore, the apprehension of the object that is other than that [non-existent thing] is also accepted as a means of proving its non-existence.
But it is not by way of being a logical mark (*liṅga*),
because even in that case, if non-existence were to be established separately,
the absence of a relationship would be equal [to the previous case]. At the very time when the logical mark manifests, there is the absence of that [relationship].

Because [the absence] is established [by that very cognition]. For one does not first apprehend the existence of something else, establish its positive and negative concomitances (*anvaya-vyatireka*) for the sake of that apprehension, and then subsequently apprehend the absence of that [other thing]. Rather, one apprehends the absence of that very thing precisely while apprehending what is other than it.
Because, immediately after perception and without any intervention, one establishes that "this exists" and "this does not exist";
and because the illustrative example is unestablished. And that which is its mark (liṅga) is...

That [reason] which possesses both positive and negative concomitance cannot be demonstrated in this way: that "wherever there is the perception of another thing, there is the absence of that [first thing]," because the perception of that [other thing] alone does not occur anywhere.

Because [the absence] is not established. Even when the example is presented in a general manner, since there too is an absence of any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that very perception of the existence of something else serves as the prover of the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*).
Thus, because the example would never reach a final conclusion, there is no comprehension [of the probandum].

Therefore, the establishment of non-existence does not result from any logical mark (*liṅga*). That "existence of another" (*anyabhāva*), established through non-perception characterized as perception (*pratyakṣa-lakṣaṇa-anupalambha*), may establish the conventional usage of non-existence for the sake of those who are deluded; enough with this digression.
This non-apprehension is threefold: when the causal relation (kāryakāraṇabhāva) is established, there is the non-apprehension of the cause;

when the pervaded-pervader relation (vyāpyavyāpakabhāva) is established, there is the non-apprehension of the pervader whose absence is established; and there is also the non-apprehension of the essential nature (svabhāvānupalabdhi).

In that case, even for the cause and the pervader, the establishment of the conventional usage of "non-existence" regarding their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) occurs precisely through the establishment of the existence of something else. When that [intrinsic nature] is unestablished there, it proves either the absence of the effect and the pervaded, or the conventional usage of their non-existence. However, in the case of the non-perception of intrinsic nature, it is by means of non-perception itself.
By means of that which serves as a logical mark (*liṅga*), it is precisely the conventional usage of non-existence (*abhāva-vyavahāra*) that is established.
If the cause or the pervader [is not perceived], then through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*)— which consists in the establishment of the existence of something other than them—
the conventional usage of non-existence regarding another thing is established, and its non-existence is proven.

And for one who establishes that [non-existence], that non-perception is the means of establishing the conventional usage of "non-existent" only when [the object] has reached the conditions for perceptibility;
how then could it apply to those two when they are beyond the senses?
The application [of the reason] is with respect to the object. This application is not [itself] a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because the logical mark (*liṅga*) is not ascertained.
It is merely that, if there is an absence of the cause and the pervader whose relationship is established, [then the effect and the pervaded are absent].
These two [reasons] are employed for the purpose of demonstrating that the non-existence of the other [alternative] is necessarily ascertained.
Thus, this property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), which possesses both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekavat*), being pervaded by a portion thereof,
is a three-characterized (*trilakṣaṇa*) or three-formed (*trirūpa*) reason that makes its own probandum known.
Because of the non-deviation from the property (*dharma*),

others maintain that the logical reason (*hetu*) has six characteristics. These three— namely, having an uncontradicted object, being intended as a single number, and being known— [are included therein].

In this regard, the property of having an uncontradicted object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) does not constitute a separate definition, because there is a contradiction between contradiction (*bādha*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). For invariable concomitance is the presence of the reason (*hetu*) only when the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) exists. That reason, possessing such a characteristic, would exist in the subject (*dharmin*); in this case—
And how could that [property] not be the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*)? For when perception and inference subvert the property to be proven, they expel it from that locus (*dharmin*);
whereas the reason (*hetu*), existing only when that [property] is present, establishes it right there in that locus.
Alas, what a great instability there is among entities!

If it is argued that the reason (*hetu*) which is inseparably connected (*avinābhāvī*) with the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*) does not reside in the subject (*dharmin*) itself, then why is this wretched man seeking a son after marrying a eunuch? For him—

Even if the subject (*dharmin*) does not exist, how can it be said that "that subject possesses the property to be proven" (*sādhya-dharma*) by demonstrating the presence [of that property] therein? For this very reason, the absence of sublation (*bādhā*) has been stated. This might be the case:

Since the reason itself might occur otherwise [i.e., even in the absence of the property to be proven], for that very reason it is said that the subject possesses a property uncontradicted by the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore,
what now is the efficacy of the reason, since the probandum is established by the non-contradiction alone?

If the absence of the probandum is necessarily present when sublation by a valid means of cognition occurs, then the establishment of the probandum occurs only when there is no sublation; thus, the logical reason (hetu) is useless, for it remains so even in the case of sublation.

Because there is an absence of the capacity for proof; and if there were no restriction, there would be no subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), and the non-existence of the probandum (*sādhya*) would be possible— thus, there is no capacity for non-subversion.

Non-sublation (*abādhā*) is not the absence of sublation; rather, it is the non-perception of sublation. And since that [non-perception] might occur for a person even when sublation is possible in some cases, it is the domain of the employment of the logical reason (*hetu*). Is the logical reason, then, [employed] even when sublation is perceived?
It is not afraid of sublation;
for if it were, one would have to employ non-perception even while disregarding sublation. Therefore, that reason is [valid] in the ultimate sense.
Without regard to whether sublation exists or does not exist, [the reason] should be employed when no sublation is perceived.
For what purpose is it employed? For the sake of establishing the probandum (*sādhya*). Would it then establish the probandum even when sublation is present in some cases?

Because of this, no effort is made toward the ascertainment of its non-existence, and a logical reason (*hetu*) is employed. Consequently, "having a subject that is not sublated" (*abādhitaviṣayatva*) cannot be a defining characteristic of a valid reason, since sublation (*bādhā*) [is possible].
Even when it exists, this [non-perception] functions by virtue of its capacity;
