and likewise, since activity is impossible for one who is in doubt without such acceptance, just as in the case of non-perception where there is the possibility of the existence of a sublation (*bādhā*).
Even if it were granted that [the reason] is employed [in the case of non-apprehension],
it should likewise be employed in the case of sublation and apprehension as well.
Because there is no distinction [in the case] of its acceptance.

If it is argued that there is no capacity when sublation (*bādhā*) exists, then if this were so, even that which has been employed would result in a lack of capacity; thus, the possibility of sublation remains undetermined.

It does not deserve to be employed. If it is argued that its capacity [to invalidate] exists when no sublation (*bādha*) is perceived, does perception pervade sublation, such that there could be the possibility of sublation for the reason (*hetu*)?

The incapacity [of the reason] that has been established would not be possible. If, on the other hand, the sublation ceases upon the cessation of that [incapacity], even so, since the probandum is established simply from the non-perception of sublation, the reason is useless; for when there is no perception [of sublation], sublation is impossible. Upon the cessation of perception...

Furthermore, if sublation (bādhā) has not been removed, the incapacity of the reason remains as it was; thus, it is not to be employed. Therefore, even if the reason occurs otherwise—neither through the presence nor the absence of its own probandum—it effects nothing in the subject (dharmin), nor does it cause anything to be absent there.
The objection is not valid. Therefore, non-sublation (*abādha*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) do not coexist;
consequently, non-sublation is not a distinct characteristic (*rūpāntara*).
Thus, it is for the purpose of adopting a different definition that a further qualification is required.
Or it might be that when one thing exists, another thing is absent. For example:

"presence in the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) and "presence in the similar class" (*sapakṣe bhāva*). However, this is not possible when there is an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with the sublation (*bādhā*); therefore, [the fallacies] of the contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*) and the non-differentiation from the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyayāvibhāvin*) do not apply here.

Since sublation (*bādhā*) is possible regarding the object (*viṣaya*), its absence need not be stated as a separate definition for these two. Therefore, when the reason (*hetu*) is employed, there is no possibility of faults in the thesis (*pratijñā*); nor is the thesis alone [sufficient].
Therefore, the faults of the thesis (*pratijñā-doṣa*) need not be stated.

By this, the intention to express a singular number (*eka-saṃkhyā-vivakṣā*) is also refuted. How so? For that which is one is non-deviant from its own state of being the probandum (*sva-sādhya-bhāva*) precisely because it exists as such; whereas anything other than that [is deviant].
Because there exists precisely that which sublates it, [the claim that] "it is contradictory to that" is equal [in status] to [the claim made by] the sublater (*bādhā*).
Furthermore, is that [correct cognition] one for which a counter-reason (*pratihetu*) is impossible in reality? It is correct cognition.
Is it a reason based on a contrary [reason], or is it one for which a counter-reason has not been shown? And what follows from this?
If it is a case where a counter-reason is impossible, then because it cannot be ascertained, it lacks the defining characteristic [of a valid reason].

This is [the case]. Or rather, it is the absence of a reason (*hetv-abhāva*). For a property that serves as a means of proof (*pratipādaka-dharma*) whose nature is not certain cannot possess the definition of a [valid] reason, just as [a property] whose presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is doubtful does not;
nor can a reason have a doubtful definition. Thus, there is no reason at all.
It would be so. For the occurrence of a counter-correlative (pratiyogin) is observed in cases where the characteristics are identical;
this gives rise to doubt even regarding those things whose counter-correlatives have not been observed, because there is no distinction [between them]. Or, if [such a distinction] were present...

The definition of a reason (*hetu*) applies specifically to this [type of reason], for it is by means of this that a reason—being entirely free from counter-arguments—ascertains its own probandum (*sādhya*). Therefore, that which lacks this definition would not be a valid reason. And thus:

The intention to express a single number [in the definition] would be redundant. Consequently, the definition of the "non-deviant contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) would be lost, because the term "non-deviant contradictory" applies when two reasons, each possessing its own specific characteristic, are presented in contradiction with one another regarding a single subject (*dharmin*). Furthermore, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of that particular [fallacy] is not...

It is pointed out that we perceive the possibility or impossibility of counter-correlatives (pratiyogin) based on [certain conditions]. Therefore, because there is doubt in every case that no distinction exists at all, [the opponent argues as follows].
It must be so;

for even in the case of a reason that has a perceived counter-reason (*pratihetu*), no distinction whatsoever is observed prior to [the appearance of] the other. Nor is it the case that those reasons which have possible counter-reasons are always [invalid].
Its apprehension exists;
however, superior wisdom is observed to be imaginative. Therefore, because there is no certainty regarding possibility and impossibility, the definition [of the means of knowledge] is not certain.
There might be some reason [for this]. Alternatively, it may be that the counter-reason has not been demonstrated, as it was said:
"In that case, when [the property of] being sound..."
If one accepts that it is eternal,
then this would indeed be the reason, provided that there is impermanence in this case.
"No one would show the reason, such as 'being produced' (kṛtakatva) and so forth. This is a most grievous calamity that has arrived—one that is both impossible to reveal and impossible to conceal.
How could it possibly be endured? For the time being, this reason [applies] to entities...

Having established their own respective objects of proof as the fundamental nature [of reality], and having endowed those persons who take them as authoritative with both worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), a person possessed of inspired intuition (*pratibhāvatā*)—
by means of other reasons and illustrations— renders the efficacy of those proofs obstructed.
Having caused those things and those persons to fall away from their excellence of being—that is, like a king deprived of his kingdom, he goes to the forest of asceticism—what can we say about this?
Furthermore, the status of being a means is produced by human intuition; so, is that [means] real in fact?
Whether it be a proof or not a proof, that logical reason (hetu) exists by its very nature as possessing that property;
how then could it be made otherwise? For there can be no alteration of the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of real entities.
And because both [the probandum and the probans] lack a contradictory nature, how could that which possesses a property not belonging to it ever be a means of proof for anything else? Therefore,
[the two types of reason] possess by their very nature an inseparable connection with their own respective probanda, as defined above.
Because a counter-reason possessing those same characteristics cannot exist for either an effect or an essential nature, the intention to express a singular number is not a defining characteristic,
since there is nothing to be excluded.

Furthermore, if cognition does not possess the nature of a logical mark (*liṅga*), how will it have the characteristics of a logical mark? When considering what kind of logical mark the object is to be known from,
the form of that which is non-discrepant for the cognizer is stated.
Upon seeing which,
one distinguishes between the means of proof and what is not, and based on the conviction that the desired object is present, one undertakes activity. Likewise, that which is its essential nature—

It is the definition [of the means of knowledge], not the nature of another. If being its definition were based merely on its utility in the production of cognition, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). In that case, even objects of knowledge (*prameya*), persons (*puruṣa*), and so forth, would become its definitions.
For indeed, in the absence of those [reasons], there can be no cognition of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*).
If that is so, then the term "ascertained" (*niścita*) need not be employed. It is not that it need not be employed;
for it serves another purpose. Through the observation and non-observation in the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*), [the reason] becomes a means of comprehension.

For those who maintain that a cause must exist, a reason is not at all capable [of proving its conclusion], because it is observed that even when presence and absence are both present, there is no demonstration [of the probandum]. Therefore, the term "ascertained" (niścita) is employed for the purpose of making known that [the reason] demonstrates [the probandum] through the existence and non-existence [of the subject]. By this, the nature of another...
It is not a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*),
because it does not denote a specific form of the logical mark (*liṅga*); for those two—
existence and non-existence— are to be understood through the operation that establishes their respective states.
Because there is no other means [to establish it]. Therefore,
even if it were established merely by the statement of existence or non-existence, [it would not suffice].
Since valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is being questioned,
the word "ascertained" (*niścita*) is employed in the definition in order to establish those two.

Otherwise, since the establishment of the existence of an object of cognition (jñeya) is based upon the existence of its cognition, the very proof of the existence of those two [the cognition and the object] would entail that the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) which establishes their existence must function everywhere as the means for establishing the existence [of all things]. This is because [cognition] is for the sake of another.
And regarding the composition of this treatise: those who do not know that the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpa-liṅga*) is the means of verifying an object,
they will not engage [with it] on its basis.
Although cognition is established because it is perceived by another [cognition],
nevertheless,
some establish those very two— existence and non-existence— by means of mere perception and non-perception.
The word "ascertained" (niścita) is stated for the purpose of excluding that [uncertainty],
because there is doubt regarding existence even when presence and absence (anvaya-vyatireka) are present. Therefore, since existence—
We have included these [two terms] for the purpose of making it known that the ascertainment of these two depends upon the establishing means of valid cognition (*prasādhaka-pramāṇa*).
This is because the establishment of the implication of those proving means of cognition is accomplished merely by stating existence and non-existence.
Knowledge distinct from this [inference] does not constitute a defining characteristic [of the object],
because the object is already understood by that very [inference],

just like the meaning of the application (upanaya), since it possesses the property of being a predicate of the subject (pakṣadharmatva). This applies to both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
If it is argued that there is nevertheless no distinctness because both [the presence and absence] are understood from the application of a single [reason],
we say no; for the existence and non-existence of the reason in the similar and dissimilar instances are not mutually...

[It is] by implication (*ākṣepāt*); it is said that a single sentence conveys both [meanings], not that one meaning [is the literal sense] of the second. If it is argued that there is mutual implication (*parasparākṣepa*) in the sentence, "Indeed, [the thing] exists when that [other] exists, and it does not exist when that is absent," [we reply:]...

This statement, even though it belongs to a single [term] that indicates a restriction, implies both [existence and non-existence] by its own force, because the implication of the second is inseparable from it; it does not, however, imply existence and non-existence as two independent entities.
And these two are not independent, because restriction possesses a dual nature.
Therefore, when it is said that "existence is only there," it is not meant that existence itself [is restricted].

Nor is the other [the non-existence] simply a non-entity (abhāva), such that existence or non-existence would imply a second [category]. Knowledge is not thus distinct from the three characteristics because of the observation of another; therefore, there is no separate characteristic.
Therefore, the reason does not possess six characteristics.
The *Hetubindu*, composed by the master Dharmakīrti, is completed.
